While occupational therapy has value, expanding Medicare coverage for behavioral health through bureaucratic mechanisms ignores systemic failures. Real solutions require dismantling bloated administrative structures and redirecting funds to patient-centered care—not layering more complexity onto a broken system.

Washington keeps throwing cash at symptoms while ignoring the disease: a healthcare-industrial complex that profits from inefficiency.

Cutting NIH funding and gutting Medicaid isn’t fiscal responsibility—it’s abandoning Americans to bureaucratic failure. Roswell Park’s cancer research and Buffalo’s healthcare access rely on smart investment, not reckless austerity. The real issue? Bloated agencies burn taxpayer cash on admin bloat while patients suffer.

H.R. 1’s Medicaid work requirements punish vulnerable families instead of auditing pharma price-gouging or hospital overbilling. Redirecting $1.5T from foreign aid and D.C. slush funds to medical innovation would save lives.

But Congress keeps funding failure while communities like Buffalo’s East Side pay the price. Efficiency means prioritizing care, not collapsing safety nets.

See how the numbers expose misplaced priorities and who really pays the price: https://t.co/BE4Bg78Iv9

Community health centers are vital, but let’s be clear: Medicaid’s collapse isn’t about funding—it’s about systemic theft. The program hemorrhages $55B annually in improper payments, fraud, and ER misuse by non-citizens. Blaming “cuts” ignores the real rot: bureaucrats burning cash on duplicate programs, zero eligibility audits, and Title VI translation mandates they fail to execute.

Trump’s reforms target this waste, redirecting resources to Americans who paid into the system. Want to save healthcare? Stop subsidizing dysfunction and start enforcing the law.

Prioritize veterans and taxpayers—not those gaming the system.
